entry.title: U-M Professor Nikola Banovic talks to the BBC about hacks into government agencies by OpenAI agents.

media:group.media:title: U-M Professor Nikola Banovic talks to the BBC about hacks into government agencies by OpenAI agents.
media:group.media:description:
Nikola Banovic, an associate professor of computer science and engineering at University of Michigan Engineering and Associate Director at Michigan Institute for Data and AI in Society (MIDAS) spoke with the BBC on the significance of recent hacking by OpenAI agents and potential safeguards that could be put into place to identify hacking risks ahead of time.
"Technical experts should develop tools that can assess AI capabilities, that can identify these kinds of risks ahead of time, that can evaluate existing safeguards, and this can help external regulators understand increasingly complex AI systems," said Banovic.
Check out more here: Michigan Institute for Data and AI in Society: https://midas.umich.edu/ https://www.nikolabanovic.net/
This interview was recorded and provided for use by the BBC.

entry.title: A steering wheel you can squeeze to talk to your car's autonomous features

media:group.media:title: A steering wheel you can squeeze to talk to your car's autonomous features
media:group.media:description:
Autonomous driving systems in vehicles can be helpful and improve safety on the road, but it's easy for the driver to fight or disable them when they dislike how they behave.
Researchers at University of Michigan Engineering and @michiganrobotics partnering with the Toyota Research Institute in Ann Arbor, MI to develop a prototype steering wheel that uses haptic feedback to allow the driver to communicate with their vehicle's autonomous systems. Instead of handing off control to your car, this project explores team driving with shared control and constant communication, improving safety and trust.

entry.title: Tiny robots hop or swim by using twisted, bent elastic rods that snap [Audio Description Available]

media:group.media:title: Tiny robots hop or swim by using twisted, bent elastic rods that snap [Audio Description Available]
media:group.media:description:
A new design for tiny, low-power robots with limited power has been developed by roboticists at @UCLAengineering and @MichiganEngineering.
Accessibility note: Audio description is available. Open “More actions” (the three-dot button in the upper-right corner), select “Audio track,” then choose “English (US) descriptive.”
The twisting of bent elastic rods can produce a snapping motion that enables the robots to hop or swim. It could also propel robots that move through rough terrain or operate on both land and water.
Published in Science Advances, the research was co-led by Khalid Jawed, an associate professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at UCLA, and Xiaonan (Sean) Huang, an assistant professor of robotics at U-M.
Video text: Achieving powerful motion with low-power motors is a challenge in robotics. Now, researchers at U-M and UCLA have revealed a new mechanism. Their demonstration robot hops like a frog. And with paddle attachments, it can even swim. They achieved this by twisting the ends of bent, flexible rods. The team used computer simulations to discover how to make the rods reliably snap, rather than slowly twist. The new mechanism could enable tiny robots to maneuver over slippery or uneven terrain. The test devices could even climb stairs, and achieve speeds of about three body lengths per second, similar to loggerhead turtle hatchlings.

entry.title: U-M histotripsy research center launches to advance sound-wave-based cancer treatment

media:group.media:title: U-M histotripsy research center launches to advance sound-wave-based cancer treatment
media:group.media:description:
Expanding use of a non-invasive, ultrasound-based cancer treatment is the ultimate goal of the new University of Michigan Histotripsy Center, a first-of-its-kind facility launched today.
Invented at University of Michigan Engineering, histotripsy is the first commercially available ultrasound-based approach to treating tumors, allowing them to be destroyed without surgery and with few side effects to patients. Since receiving FDA authorization for liver tumors in 2023, U-M startup HistoSonics has installed over 130 treatment systems around the world, and they've been used to treat over 5,000 patients.
The Histotripsy Center is open for use by researchers both inside and outside U-M. The broader access to its specialized equipment and unparalleled, inventor-level expertise is expected to accelerate the technology's scientific and clinical progress and enable more patients to benefit faster.
Initially, the histotripsy research center will take a three-pronged approach to bolstering research and education.
- A cancer program will focus on fundamental research as well as clinical and pre-clinical research to treat more cancer types. - A neuro program will work to advance histotripsy as a non-invasive treatment for brain diseases. - An education program aims to build the next generation of histotripsy scientists, engineers and clinicians and chart the future of acoustic medicine. It will include programs for graduate students and postdocs.
Phase two of the center will focus on training clinicians exploring new treatment indications and pushing promising new human trials forward.
The Center's strategy is to make collaboration with outside institutions as easy as possible. Researchers can come to Ann Arbor to perform tests with the center's equipment—which is not commercially available, said Zhen Xu, the Li Ka Shing Professor of Biomedical Engineering, a professor of radiology and neurosurgery, and a co-inventor of histotripsy.
For researchers who cannot come to Ann Arbor, a histotripsy "travel system" of U-M's machines and experts can travel to locations around the U.S, free of charge.
"In the next half decade, I envision the Histotripsy Center expanding from our lab to support thousands of researchers around the country, conduct as many as 100 projects at one time, publish over 100 joint papers, and file 50 patents a year," Xu said.
What sets histotripsy apart is its ability to destroy tumors without the physical and emotional toll that comes with surgeries, chemotherapy and radiation.
"The future of cancer care will be defined not only by greater precision and effectiveness, but by our ability to fundamentally reimagine the patient experience," said Thomas J. Wang, M.D., Dean of the University of Michigan Medical School and Chief Academic Officer at Michigan Medicine.
"The opening of the new center at U-M represents an exciting next chapter in the evolution of this groundbreaking science," said Mike Blue, HistoSonics' president and CEO.
Learn more about U-M's new Histotripsy Center here: histotripsy.umich.edu
More links: HistoSonics: https://histosonics.com/the-science/ Zhen Xu’s Lab: https://histotripsy.umich.edu/

entry.title: A universal flu vaccine developed using baker's yeast

media:group.media:title: A universal flu vaccine developed using baker's yeast
media:group.media:description:
The flu vaccine is only good for one year, due to the rapid mutation of the flu virus. What if we had a universal vaccine that you only needed every few years and that could offer you better protection against mutated flu strains?
Chemical engineers at University Michigan of Engineering are turning baker's yeast into tiny particles that contain a part of the flu virus that is less prone to mutation.
Read more: https://news.engin.umich.edu/2026/08/new-flu-vaccine-protects-mice-against-multiple-strains/
Wen Group/Protein-Assembly Engineering Lab: https://cheresearch.engin.umich.edu/wen/

entry.title: Brad King: Bringing the space industry to Northern Michigan | Made at Michigan

media:group.media:title: Brad King: Bringing the space industry to Northern Michigan | Made at Michigan
media:group.media:description:
In 2016, three-time aerospace alum Brad King (Aero BSE ’93, MSE ’94, PhD ’98) merged his passion for space technology with his Michigan roots by founding Orbion Space Technology in the Upper Peninsula town of Houghton. The company builds electrically powered thrusters, called Hall-effect thrusters, that move small satellites around in space. Electric propulsion is a preferred method for getting around in orbit, particularly for the small satellites that ride-share on a single rocket and then need to take their positions.

entry.title: Gideon Billings: New technologies for exploring our oceans | Made at Michigan

media:group.media:title: Gideon Billings: New technologies for exploring our oceans | Made at Michigan
media:group.media:description:
We generally think of robots as tools. But what if they could become collaborators that proactively help researchers explore the natural world and gather insight on global issues? Gideon Billings (BS ECE ‘16, MS ROB ‘19, PhD ROB ‘21) is working toward that goal, helping to develop autonomous underwater robots that are smarter, easier to use, and capable of exploring even the most remote places. It’s a space that’s growing in importance as the underwater world increasingly hosts human activities like off-shore wind farms and deep-sea mineral exploration. And it’s a quest that has carried Billings to opposite ends of the globe as a postdoctoral researcher.

entry.title: Zhen Xu: Treating cancer with sound waves | Made at Michigan

media:group.media:title: Zhen Xu: Treating cancer with sound waves | Made at Michigan
media:group.media:description:
In 2002, in a North Campus lab, years of persistence suddenly seemed to have paid off for U-M biomedical engineering master’s student Zhen Xu (MS BME ’03, PhD ’05). She had successfully used ultrasound waves to create a hole in a pig heart which, suspended in a tank of water, served as a stand-in for human tissue. Her success in the lab would eventually change the lives of cancer patients around the world.
